one_liner: First-order (ADMM) conic solver in C; on large LPs at 1e-4 accuracy it beats Clarabel, HiGHS and PDLP in its author's campaign.
what_it_does: Solves convex quadratic cone programs (min 1/2 x'Px + c'x subject to Ax + s = b, s in K) over zero, linear, box, second-order, semidefinite, complex semidefinite, exponential, power and spectral cones. The C API is scs_init / scs_solve / scs_update / scs_finish on CSC matrices plus a cone struct, and it is the backend behind the Python, Julia (SCS.jl), R, MATLAB and Ruby interfaces and CVXPY's default solver for SDP, exponential-cone and power-cone problems. It is not a drop-in for an interior-point code: you switch solvers in CVXPY or JuMP, or reformulate the data for the C API.
how_it_is_fast: Douglas-Rachford splitting (ADMM) on a homogeneous self-dual embedding (O'Donoghue et al., JOTA 2016; SIAM J. Optim. 2021), so each iteration is one linear solve with a fixed quasi-definite KKT matrix plus a cone projection. The matrix is factored once (AMD + QDLDL by default, or MKL Pardiso, cuDSS on GPU, Apple Accelerate, or matrix-free CG with eigCG deflation) and reused until the adaptive scaling changes it. Type-I Anderson acceleration (Zhang, O'Donoghue, Boyd, SIAM J. Optim. 2020) and adaptive per-row diagonal rescaling cut the iteration count. Iterations are cheap at moderate accuracy, so very large LPs reach 1e-4 sooner than with interior-point codes, which pay for a fresh factorization at every iteration.
when_to_use: Very large sparse LPs or QPs (millions of nonzeros) where 1e-4 relative accuracy is enough and interior-point or simplex codes run out of time or memory: on the Mittelmann set it verified 28 of 37 on an A100 and 24 on CPU, against 20 for Clarabel.

Problems with exponential, power, spectral or large semidefinite cones that interior-point solvers cannot fit in memory (Clarabel was killed at 64 GB on equalG11, maxG55, maxG60 and others, which SCS attempted).
Sequences of related solves: scs_update changes b and c and warm-starts while keeping the factorization.
GPU acceleration of a direct-factorization first-order method through the cuDSS backend (needs a source build).
When you need infeasibility or unboundedness certificates checked against the data: SCS returns Farkas rays and certified 24 of 29 infeasible Netlib LPs at 1e-4.
when_not_to_use: Small and medium QPs or LPs, or anything that needs 1e-6 or tighter: over all 157 QPs Clarabel (3.1 s) and PIQP (3.7 s) beat SCS CPU (7.5 s) in shifted geometric mean, and HiGHS beats it on all 349 LPs (5.0 s against 11.9 s).

Small or medium SDPs: SCS was last in geometric mean on the 94 SDPs (107.5 s against 38.2 s for SDPA), and on badly conditioned control, truss and gpp instances it ran hundreds of thousands of iterations; the GPU does not help there because the eigendecompositions dominate.
Badly scaled problems where a reported 'solved' must be trusted: QGROW7, QGROW22 and neos-4413714-turia returned false certificates when the diagonal rescaling hit its floor.
Platforms without the MKL wheel (aarch64, macOS, Windows, musllinux) fall back to single-threaded QDLDL, so the published CPU numbers do not carry over directly.
Exact or vertex solutions (basis, sensitivity data): use a simplex code such as HiGHS.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (Make or CMake), plus PyPI and conda-forge Python packages and other language bindings
integration.dependencies: none for LP/QP/SOCP and exponential/power cones (AMD from SuiteSparse and QDLDL are vendored in linsys/external); BLAS/LAPACK for SDP and spectral cones (USE_LAPACK=1 by default); optional Intel MKL, NVIDIA CUDA + cuDSS, Apple Accelerate; Python wheel needs numpy and scipy
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (CMAKE_C_STANDARD 99), CMake 3.22+ or GNU make; Python 3.9+ for the wheel
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows on x86-64 and aarch64; the MKL Pardiso backend ships only in x86-64 manylinux wheels; cuDSS and GPU-indirect need an NVIDIA GPU and a source build
integration.thread_safety: Not documented as such; each solve owns its ScsWork workspace, and the process-wide Ctrl-C handler is reference-counted under a mutex. USE_OPENMP=1 parallelizes matrix multiplies (off by default).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — in CVXPY or JuMP switching from Clarabel is a one-argument solver change, but the native C API, tolerance semantics (eps_abs/eps_rel, default 1e-4) and accuracy differ

gotchas: Harness finding: the record's caveat says SCS CPU ran 4-thread MKL Pardiso against single-threaded rivals. But the scs-python 3.3.1 README and meson.build say the x86-64 manylinux wheel statically links sequential MKL (libmkl_sequential.a, 'single-threaded'), so OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 does not parallelize Pardiso. The CPU linear solves were therefore most likely single-threaded too, which makes that comparison fairer than the record states. Only BLAS calls such as the SDP eigendecompositions could use more threads.

Harness finding: the GPU row is not the PyPI 3.3.1 release the page names. tools/bench_modal.py builds it with 'git clone --recursive --depth 1' of scs-python HEAD (unpinned, -Dlink_cudss=true -Dint32=true) against an unpinned apt cuDSS on a CUDA 12.6 image, so the exact SCS code version behind 208 s is not recorded in the harness.

The defaults are eps_abs = eps_rel = 1e-4 and max_iters = 100000. Tighten both for accurate answers and raise max_iters for long runs; a 'solved' status on a badly scaled problem can still fail an independent residual check.

linear_solver=AUTO picks MKL Pardiso only in the x86-64 Linux wheel (QDLDL elsewhere, and QDLDL even on macOS where Accelerate is available). cuDSS needs 32-bit indices (-Dint32=true), and spectral cones need USE_SPECTRAL_CONES=1.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick SCS over PIQP, ProxQP or QPALM when the problem is a very large LP/QP at moderate (1e-4) accuracy, needs non-QP cones (SDP, exponential, power), or should run on a GPU through cuDSS. Prefer PIQP (or Clarabel) for small and medium QPs and for 1e-6 or tighter, where the interior-point codes were faster in this same campaign.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's own campaign on the 37 Mittelmann LPs at 1e-4 (1800 s limit, failures charged 5400 s), the shifted geometric mean was 208 s with 28 verified solves for SCS with cuDSS on an A100, and 431 s with 24 solves for SCS CPU (PyPI wheel, MKL Pardiso backend, 4-core AMD EPYC Milan Modal container). Clarabel 0.11.1 took 817 s (20 solves), OR-Tools PDLP 733 s and HiGHS 2889 s, all run from prebuilt wheels with no compiler flags stated and every solution re-checked against the data. On the largest QP quartile SCS CPU is level with Clarabel (12.8 s against 12.6 s), and the author's own QTQP, which the page omits, beat SCS GPU (192 s against 208 s).
status_note: Actively maintained (3.3.1 on PyPI 2026-09-05, commits into October 2026) and MIT-licensed with OSI-licensed vendored AMD and QDLDL, so it can be vendored. The evidence stays first-party (tier C), and the GPU row ran an unpinned source build rather than the named release; the record's 4-thread caveat looks wrong because the wheel's MKL is sequential.
